output:
Field notes

Three things self-hosting exposed

Every one of them presented as a symptom that pointed somewhere other than its cause. If you are standing up your own instance, you will probably meet at least one.

These came out of running the thing somewhere other than where it was built. That is the whole value of self-hosting as a test: it removes the assumptions that only held because there was one deployment. What follows is each fault as you will actually encounter it, then what it really was.

OneEvery MCP call returns unauthorized

What you see
unauthorized on every call, immediately, with a key you just minted.
Where it points
The signature. You go and check clock skew, canonicalisation, header casing, the secret itself.
What it is
The right key sent to the wrong host.

The MCP client shipped with a hardcoded default base URL — the original deployment's. A self-hoster who followed /start by hand ended up installing a client that dutifully signed its requests and sent them to somebody else's host, one that had never seen that key and had no reason to accept it.

So the rejection was correct. The request was well-formed, the signature was valid, and the recipient was a stranger. Nothing in the error tells you that, because from the server's point of view an unknown key and a bad signature are the same refusal.

Fix

The instance now substitutes its own URL when it serves the client file, which is how /cli already worked. A client downloaded from your deployment talks to your deployment. If you are diagnosing this on an older install, check the base URL in the installed client before you check anything cryptographic:

grep -n 'https://' <path-to-installed-mcp-client>

The general lesson: a default that is invisible and correct for exactly one user is not a default, it is a hardcoded value with good manners.

TwoThe claude mcp add command on /start arrives as one line

What you see
The copyable command on the setup page is a single joined line. Backslashes that should break it across lines are gone.
Where it points
Whitespace handling in the renderer, or the clipboard, or the browser eating newlines.
What it is
A template literal treating the trailing backslash as a line continuation.

Inside a JavaScript template literal, a lone backslash at end of line is an escape for the newline — a line continuation. It does not survive into the string as a backslash, and it takes the newline with it. The two lines join, the continuation character vanishes, and the output looks like someone deliberately wrote one long command.

// wrong — backslash and newline both disappear
const cmd = `claude mcp add sirdocalot \
  --transport http https://example.invalid/mcp`;

// right — escape the backslash
const cmd = `claude mcp add sirdocalot \\
  --transport http https://example.invalid/mcp`;

The tell is that nothing looks broken. There is no error and no missing character in any obvious sense; the string is simply shorter than the source that produced it. It is one of the few bugs where the source code is more readable than the output it generates, which is exactly backwards from how you normally hunt.

Fix

Double the backslash. And if a template literal is emitting shell, treat every trailing backslash in it as suspect until you have read it in the rendered page rather than the editor.

ThreeA numeric env var is set but has no effect

What you see
You set MAX_AWAIT_MS=90s. Behaviour is unchanged from the default. No warning, no log line.
Where it points
The variable not reaching the process — wrong env file, wrong container, restart not applied.
What it is
The value arrived, failed to parse, and was silently replaced by the default.

90s is not a number. The loader parsed it, got nothing usable, and fell back — so MAX_AWAIT_MS=90s quietly became ninety milliseconds' worth of default behaviour rather than the ninety seconds you meant. You would only find out by reading the loader.

What makes this worse than an ordinary papered-over error is where it lived: in a config loader whose entire stated posture is refusing loudly. A component that promises to fail hard on bad input, and then does not, is more dangerous than one that never made the promise, because you stop checking.

Fix

It refuses now. An unparseable numeric environment variable is a startup failure, named, with the offending value shown. Silent fallback is only acceptable when the variable is absent — the absence of a setting is a decision, a malformed setting is a mistake.

And one guardA shared class redefined by a page stylesheet

Not a self-hosting bug, but the same shape, and it has now bitten twice.

What you see
Every input inside a preview renders uppercase and tiny.
Where it points
The block renderer, or the preview component, or the input styling.
What it is
The gallery page defined .label. The block renderer uses .label for a field label. The page stylesheet won.

Both times it was found by eye. Finding a class collision by noticing that some text looks wrong is not a method — it is luck with a good memory attached. So there is now a test that asserts no page stylesheet redefines a class the shared stylesheet defines.

The important part is the last step: the guard was proved to bite before it was trusted. A test that would not have caught the original bug is worse than no test, because it converts an open question into a settled one. Reintroduce the collision, watch the test fail, remove it, watch it pass. Only then does it count.

The thread through all four: each symptom was a faithful report of a downstream effect, and each cause sat one layer up from where the report pointed. unauthorized is true. The joined command is what the string actually contained. The default really was in effect. The label really was uppercase.

Nothing lied. The information was just missing at the point where you needed it — which is the argument for loud refusal at the boundary, and for guards that have been watched to fail.

Notes from self-hosting. Fixes are in; the guard is in and proven.
